chapters.1.summary: Job lives in the land of Uz and is blameless and rich. He has seven sons and three daughters and offers sacrifices for them. In heaven the accuser, called Satan, comes before the LORD. The LORD praises Job, and Satan asks whether Job fears God for nothing. The LORD lets him take all that Job has. In one day raiders, fire, and a great wind destroy his herds, servants, and children. Job tears his robe, falls to the ground, and worships. He says the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away.
chapters.1.lds: Come, Follow Me reads the heavenly exchange as poetry about an accuser’s challenge. What does verse 1 tell the reader about Job?
chapters.2.summary: Satan comes before the LORD again. He says a man will give anything to save his own skin. The LORD lets him strike Job’s body but spare his life. Job is covered with painful sores from head to foot. He sits in ashes and scrapes himself with broken pottery. His wife tells him to curse God and die. He answers that people must accept hardship from God as well as good. Three friends come to comfort him and sit with him in silence for a week.
chapters.2.lds: Come, Follow Me asks why faith should continue when expected rewards disappear. What do the friends do for seven days (verse 13)?
chapters.3.summary: After seven days Job speaks. He curses the day he was born and the night he was conceived. He wants that day turned to darkness and left out of the calendar. He asks why he did not die at birth. In the grave, he says, the weary rest and the slave is free. He asks why life is given to people in misery. What he feared most has happened. He has no ease, no quiet, and no rest.
chapters.3.lds: Come, Follow Me allows questions and faith to remain together during suffering. What does Job curse in verse 3?
chapters.4.summary: Eliphaz of Teman speaks first, and he begins gently. He says Job has taught and strengthened many people. Now trouble has reached Job, and he is shaken. Eliphaz asks who ever perished while innocent. In his experience those who sow trouble reap it. He tells of a night vision that made his bones shake. A voice asked whether a mortal can be more just than God. Even God’s servants in heaven are not beyond fault.
chapters.4.lds: Come, Follow Me asks readers to examine the friends’ claim that pain proves guilt. What does Eliphaz say has happened to Job in verse 5?
chapters.5.summary: Eliphaz continues. He says resentment kills the fool, and trouble does not grow from the ground. People are born to trouble as sparks fly upward. In Job’s place he would take his case to God. God does great things, sends rain, and lifts up the lowly. The person God corrects is happy, so Job should not reject discipline. God wounds, and he also heals. Job will yet have safety, many children, and a long life.
chapters.5.lds: Come, Follow Me questions the friends’ explanation that God is punishing Job. What does Eliphaz call Job’s suffering in verse 17?
chapters.6.summary: Job answers Eliphaz. He says his grief would outweigh the sand of the sea. The arrows of the Almighty are in him. He wishes God would crush him and end it. He says a despairing person should have kindness from a friend. His friends are like a stream that dries up in the heat. Caravans turn aside to it and find nothing. He asks them to show him plainly where he has gone wrong.
chapters.6.lds: Job asks for kindness before a verdict. How could his friends answer that request?
chapters.7.summary: Job says human life is like the hard service of a hired worker. He has months of emptiness and nights of misery. His skin is broken, and his days pass faster than a weaver’s shuttle. He turns and speaks to God directly. He asks whether he is a sea monster that needs a guard. God frightens him with dreams. He asks why God watches a human being so closely. He asks why God does not pardon him before he lies in the dust.
chapters.7.lds: Job speaks directly to God about pain. What does he ask God to change?
chapters.8.summary: Bildad of Shuah answers Job. He calls Job’s words a great wind. He asks whether God ever bends justice. If Job’s children sinned, God gave them what they earned. If Job will seek God and is pure, God will restore him. Bildad tells him to ask earlier generations. A reed without water withers, and so does the hope of the godless. God will not reject a blameless man and will yet fill Job’s mouth with laughter.
chapters.8.lds: Come, Follow Me asks what goes wrong when friends explain pain through blame. What does Bildad say about Job’s children in verse 4?
chapters.9.summary: Job agrees that no one can be in the right against God. God moves mountains, shakes the earth, and made the stars. He passes by, and Job cannot see him. Even if Job were innocent, his own mouth would condemn him. He says God destroys the blameless and the wicked alike. His days run past like a swift messenger. God is not a man whom he could meet in court. There is no umpire to lay a hand on them both.
chapters.9.lds: Job wants someone to hear both sides. What prevents him from feeling heard?
chapters.10.summary: Job says he will speak freely in his bitterness. He asks God to show him why they are in dispute. He asks whether God enjoys crushing what his own hands made. God knows that Job is not guilty. Job recalls being shaped like clay and knit together with bones. God gave him life and watched over his spirit. Yet God seems to have kept this suffering in store. Job asks to be left alone before he goes to the land of darkness.
chapters.10.lds: Job recalls the care that formed him. Why does his present pain make that memory difficult?
chapters.11.summary: Zophar of Naamah answers. He says such a flood of talk must not go unanswered. Job claims to be pure, and Zophar wishes God would speak against him. God, he says, is punishing Job less than he deserves. No one can measure the depths of God. If Job puts away sin, he will lift his face without shame. His trouble will pass like water gone by. The eyes of the wicked will fail.
chapters.11.lds: Come, Follow Me questions Zophar’s claim that Job’s pain comes from wrongdoing. What does Zophar say about what Job deserves (verse 6)?
chapters.12.summary: Job answers with sarcasm that wisdom will die with his friends. He has understanding as well as they do. He has become a joke to his neighbors, though he is upright. Robbers live in peace. Even the animals know that the LORD’s hand has done this. Wisdom and strength belong to God. He tears down, and no one rebuilds. He makes counselors, judges, and kings foolish and leads nations astray.
chapters.12.lds: Come, Follow Me asks what Job knows about God while challenging his friends. What does Job say the animals know (verses 7–9)?
chapters.13.summary: Job says he knows all that his friends know. He wants to argue his case with God himself. He calls his friends liars and useless doctors. Their silence would be their wisdom. He asks whether they will speak falsely on God’s behalf. He warns that God will rebuke them for it. He will keep to his ways before God, whatever it costs. He asks God to remove his hand and tell him his sins.
chapters.13.lds: Come, Follow Me follows the King James Bible’s reading about trusting God. How does that reading differ from the World English Bible here?
chapters.14.summary: Job says human life is short and full of trouble. A person blooms like a flower and fades like a shadow. A cut tree may sprout again at the scent of water. A person lies down and does not rise. Job wishes God would hide him in the grave until the anger passes. He asks whether someone who dies will live again. He would wait for God to call and long for him. But water wears away stone, and God wears away human hope.
chapters.14.lds: Come, Follow Me connects this question with resurrection through Jesus Christ. What does Job ask God to remember?
chapters.15.summary: Eliphaz speaks a second time, and his tone is sharper. He says Job’s words are hot wind. Job’s talk undermines reverence for God. His own mouth condemns him. Eliphaz asks whether Job was the first man born or sat in God’s council. He asks why God’s comforts are too small for Job. No human is pure before God. The wicked man lives in pain and dread and loses all he has.
chapters.15.lds: Eliphaz treats protest as proof of guilt. What happens when listeners make that assumption?
chapters.16.summary: Job calls his friends miserable comforters. He could talk as they do if they were in his place. He would instead strengthen them with his words. He says God has worn him out and torn him in anger. God set him up as a target and broke him. His face is red with weeping, though his hands are clean. He cries to the earth not to cover his blood. Even now, he says, his witness is in heaven.
chapters.16.lds: Come, Follow Me asks how friends can strengthen someone instead of adding blame. What does Job call his friends in verse 2?
chapters.17.summary: Job says his spirit is broken and the grave is ready. Mockers surround him. He asks God to put up a pledge for him, since no one else will. He has become a byword among the people. He says the upright will be appalled at this. He finds no wise man among his friends. His plans are broken off. If the grave is his home, he asks, where is his hope?
chapters.17.lds: Job’s plans have broken apart. What kind of help could reach him now?
chapters.18.summary: Bildad speaks again and is offended. He asks why Job treats his friends as stupid animals. He asks whether the earth should be rearranged for Job’s sake. The light of the wicked goes out. His own schemes throw him down, and traps wait on every side. Terrors chase him, and disease eats his skin. His tent is destroyed, and his name is forgotten. He leaves no child or descendant among his people.
chapters.18.lds: Bildad describes the loss of a name and children. How might Job hear those words?
chapters.19.summary: Job asks how long his friends will crush him with words. He says God has wronged him and closed his path. God has stripped his honor and uprooted his hope. His relatives, guests, and servants treat him as a stranger. His wife and children turn from him. He begs his friends for pity. He wishes his words were cut in rock forever. He says he knows his Redeemer lives and that he will see God.
chapters.19.lds: Come, Follow Me reads Job’s Redeemer as Jesus Christ. A redeemer saves or defends someone. What help does Job hope for?
chapters.20.summary: Zophar says Job’s insult forces him to reply. He says the joy of the wicked is short. A wicked man may rise to the sky, yet he vanishes like a dream. His children must repay the poor. Evil is sweet in his mouth and turns to poison inside him. He swallows riches and vomits them up. He crushed the poor and seized houses he did not build. Heaven exposes his guilt, and God’s anger is his portion.
chapters.20.lds: Zophar links wickedness with brief success. What evidence would challenge his claim?
chapters.21.summary: Job asks his friends to listen, and that will be their comfort. He asks why the wicked live long and grow strong. Their children are settled, and their houses are safe. They sing and dance and die in peace. They tell God to leave them alone. Job asks how often their lamp really goes out. One person dies at ease and another in bitterness, and both lie in the dust. Travelers report that the evil man is spared and buried with honor.
chapters.21.lds: Come, Follow Me studies the contrast between wicked success and faithful suffering. What does Job ask in verse 7?
chapters.22.summary: Eliphaz speaks a third time. He asks whether God gains anything from a person’s goodness. He says Job’s wickedness must be great. He accuses Job of taking pledges from the poor and stripping them. He says Job refused water, bread, and help to widows and orphans. That is why traps and terror surround him. Job should make peace with God and return to him. Then God will hear his prayers and make his ways bright.
chapters.22.lds: Come, Follow Me uses Eliphaz’s accusation to ask how friends can offer better help. What does Eliphaz accuse Job of in verse 6?
chapters.23.summary: Job says his complaint is still bitter. He wishes he knew where to find God. He would lay out his case and hear the answer. He believes God would listen and not overpower him. He looks east, west, north, and south and cannot see God. Yet God knows the way Job takes. When tested, he says, he will come out like gold. Still he is terrified, for God does whatever he chooses.
chapters.23.lds: Come, Follow Me connects Job’s search with faith during unanswered questions. What does Job wish he knew in verse 3?
chapters.24.summary: Job asks why God does not keep set times for judgment. People move boundary stones and steal flocks. They take the orphan’s donkey and the widow’s ox. The poor go naked in the cold and cling to rocks for shelter. They carry sheaves and go hungry. They tread the winepress and are thirsty. The dying groan in the city, and God charges no one. Murderers, adulterers, and thieves work in the dark.
chapters.24.lds: Come, Follow Me uses other Church scripture to study suffering. Which examples show Job’s concern for people beyond himself?
chapters.25.summary: Bildad gives the last and shortest speech of the three friends. He says rule and awe belong to God. God makes peace in his high places. His armies cannot be counted, and his light rises on everyone. Bildad asks how a human can be right before God. Even the moon and stars are not pure in God’s sight. A human being, he says, is a maggot and a worm.
chapters.25.lds: Bildad speaks about human weakness. Does his answer address what Job asked?
chapters.26.summary: Job answers Bildad with scorn. He asks how Bildad has helped the weak or advised the unwise. Then Job describes God’s power himself. The dead tremble, and the grave lies open before God. He hangs the earth on nothing. He wraps water in clouds and marks the edge of light and dark. By his power the sea is stilled. These are only the fringes of his ways, a faint whisper.
chapters.26.lds: Job asks how Bildad helped him. What separates an impressive speech from useful comfort?
chapters.27.summary: Job swears an oath by the living God, who has denied him justice. As long as he breathes, he will not speak falsely. He will never say that his friends are right. He will hold to his integrity until he dies. He asks what hope the godless have when God cuts them off. He then describes the fate of the wicked. Their children fall, and their silver passes to others. A storm sweeps them away in the night.
chapters.27.lds: Job refuses a false confession. Why would admitting his friends are right matter?
chapters.28.summary: This chapter is a poem about wisdom. People mine silver, gold, iron, and copper from the earth. Miners hang on ropes in shafts far from where anyone lives. They find sapphires where no bird or lion has gone. Yet no one knows where wisdom is found. It cannot be bought with gold or jewels. The sea and the grave do not hold it. God alone knows its place, and he says the fear of the Lord is wisdom.
chapters.28.lds: The poem separates treasure from wisdom. What can skill and wealth fail to teach?
chapters.29.summary: Job begins his last speech by remembering better days. God’s lamp shone over him, and his children were around him. When he went to the city gate, young men stepped aside and elders stood. Princes stopped talking. He rescued the poor and the orphan. He was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. He searched out the case of the stranger. People waited for his words as for rain.
chapters.29.lds: Job remembers helping people in need. How does that memory answer Eliphaz’s accusations?
chapters.30.summary: Now, Job says, younger men mock him. Their fathers were outcasts he would not have hired. He has become their song, and they spit at him. God has loosened his bowstring and humbled him. Pain gnaws his bones at night. He cries to God and gets no answer. He once wept for people in trouble, yet evil came when he hoped for good. His harp is tuned to mourning.
chapters.30.lds: Job’s neighbors add mockery to pain. What could they change without knowing why he suffers?
chapters.31.summary: Job makes his final defense as a series of oaths. If he has lied, lusted, or cheated, let him be punished. He did not reject the complaints of his servants. One God made both him and them in the womb. He shared his bread with orphans and clothed the poor. He did not trust in gold or worship the sun and moon. He did not rejoice at an enemy’s ruin. He signs his defense and asks the Almighty to answer.
chapters.31.lds: Come, Follow Me recalls Job’s repeated request for God to answer him. What does Job ask for in verse 6?
chapters.32.summary: The three friends stop answering, since Job holds that he is right. A younger man named Elihu has been listening. He is angry with Job for justifying himself and not God. He is angry with the friends for condemning Job without an answer. He waited because they were older. Now he says understanding comes from God’s Spirit, not from years. He is full of words like wine with no vent. He promises to flatter no one.
chapters.32.lds: Elihu waited for older speakers. Does his anger help him listen?
chapters.33.summary: Elihu asks Job to listen and answer if he can. He is made of clay as Job is, so Job need not fear him. He quotes Job’s claim to be innocent and wronged. He says Job is not right, for God is greater than man. God speaks in dreams to turn people from pride. He also warns through pain on a sickbed. A messenger may plead for the sick person and find a ransom. God does this again and again to bring a soul back from the pit.
chapters.33.lds: Elihu says pain can teach. How could that idea help or hurt someone in distress?
chapters.34.summary: Elihu speaks to the wise men who are listening. He quotes Job as saying God has taken away his right. He says Job drinks scorn like water and keeps company with evildoers. God cannot do wrong and repays each person’s work. If God withdrew his breath, all flesh would die. He shows no favor to princes over the poor. He sees every step and needs no inquiry. Elihu concludes that Job adds rebellion to his sin.
chapters.34.lds: Elihu defends fairness while accusing Job. What evidence supports his charge?
chapters.35.summary: Elihu asks whether Job thinks he is more right than God. He tells Job to look at the sky, far above him. Human sin does not harm God, and human goodness gives him nothing. Such things affect only other people. The oppressed cry out under the strong. Yet no one asks for God their Maker, who gives songs in the night. God does not answer an empty cry. So Job, who says he cannot see God, must wait.
chapters.35.lds: Elihu links unanswered cries with pride. What would Job’s earlier words challenge?
chapters.36.summary: Elihu says he has more to say on God’s behalf. God is mighty and despises no one. He does not keep the wicked alive, and he gives the afflicted their rights. When people are bound in suffering, he shows them their wrong. If they listen, they finish their days in good. If not, they die without knowledge. Elihu warns Job not to turn toward evil. He then praises God, who draws up water and sends rain and thunder.
chapters.36.lds: Elihu promises good years after obedience. How does that promise compare with Job’s experience?
chapters.37.summary: Elihu’s heart pounds at the thunder. He says God’s voice roars, and lightning reaches the ends of the earth. God tells the snow and the rain to fall. Animals take cover, and ice forms by God’s breath. Clouds turn wherever he guides them. Elihu tells Job to stand still and consider these works. He asks whether Job knows how clouds are balanced. He ends by saying the Almighty is beyond reach and does not oppress.
chapters.37.lds: Elihu asks about weather beyond human control. What changes when the next speaker is the Lord?
chapters.38.summary: The LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind. He asks who darkens counsel with words without knowledge. He asks where Job was when the earth’s foundations were laid. The morning stars sang then, and the sons of God shouted for joy. He asks who shut in the sea and commanded the dawn. He asks about the gates of death and the storehouses of snow. He sends rain on deserts where no one lives. He asks who feeds the lion and the raven.
chapters.38.lds: The Seminary lesson connects the joyful sons of God with life before birth. What does God ask Job about creation?
chapters.39.summary: The LORD continues to question Job about wild animals. He asks whether Job knows when mountain goats give birth. He asks who set the wild donkey free to roam the salt land. The wild ox will not plow or stay in a barn. The ostrich leaves her eggs on the ground and laughs at horse and rider. The war horse charges into battle without fear. The hawk flies south, and the eagle nests on the high cliff.
chapters.39.lds: Come, Follow Me asks how the creatures in God’s speech change the reader’s view. Who set the wild donkey free (verse 5)?
chapters.40.summary: The LORD asks whether the one who argues with the Almighty will correct him. Job answers that he is small and will say no more. The LORD speaks again from the whirlwind. He asks whether Job will condemn him in order to be right. He asks whether Job has an arm like God’s. Let Job humble every proud person and crush the wicked. Then God will admit that Job can save himself. He points to Behemoth, a huge creature that he made.
chapters.40.lds: Come, Follow Me asks readers to consider God’s creations from different views. What does God ask Job in verse 8?
chapters.41.summary: The LORD describes Leviathan, a creature of the deep. No one can catch him with a hook or make him a servant. No one will play with him like a bird or sell him in the market. Harpoons and spears are useless. His scales are like rows of sealed shields. Fire and smoke come from his mouth. Iron is like straw to him. He looks down on everything proud and is king over them.
chapters.41.lds: The poem describes Leviathan beyond human control. What does that show about the limits of power?
chapters.42.summary: Job answers the LORD. He says God can do all things. He admits that he spoke of things too wonderful for him. He had heard of God, and now his eye sees him. The LORD tells Eliphaz that the three friends did not speak rightly, as Job did. They must bring offerings, and Job will pray for them. When Job prays for his friends, the LORD restores his fortunes. Job receives twice as much, ten more children, and a long life.
chapters.42.lds: The Seminary lesson connects Job’s renewed life with hope after loss. What must the friends do after God corrects them?
